reasoning: The bob moves on a straight image line s with sustained back-and-forth oscillation and slowly shrinking envelope. With L=8.97 m fixed, frequency omega=sqrt(g/L) measures g, so candidates share that oscillator and differ from no loss to linear vs quadratic air damping to predict the held-back amplitude.

critique.finding: The bob swings back and forth like a long pendulum with pull set by {g} around center {s0} and gentle air drag set by {gamma}. It only partly captures the motion, leaving a regular wobble in its misses.
critique.headline: Pendulum swings on, air gently slowing its dance.
critique.revision_idea: Add the large-angle sine restoring force to the viscous pendulum. The leftover misses still wave back and forth with the swing, which is what a linearized pull leaves behind.
critique.why_it_won: It lets the pendulum pull change with position while bleeding speed with air, so its misses stay near noise while the airless and quadratic laws wander far.

headline: The same museum pendulum, sped up by its filmmaker: gravity comes out far too strong, so the clip plays faster than life.
finding: The bob swings back and forth like a long pendulum with pull set by about 240 m/s² around center about 320 pixel and gentle air drag set by about 0.0047 1/s. It only partly captures the motion, leaving a regular wobble in its misses. That is 25× stronger than Earth’s gravity, so the clip most likely plays about 5× faster than real life, or the stated pendulum length is not the length assumed.

eyeball.confidence: low - period ~6 s from ~3.7 swings in 22.6 s video, amplitude nearly constant, pixel scale guessed
eyeball.law_in_words: Simple pendulum period T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) with L=8.97 m, position vs time fitted as s(t)=s0+A*cos(2*pi*t/T+phi)*exp(-gamma*t)

clock.note: Gravity came out 25× too strong: the clip probably plays about 5× faster than real life (time-lapse or dropped frames), or the stated pendulum length is not the length assumed (a length read 25× too short looks the same).

clockCheck.why: Clock checked: gravity came out 25× too strong, so the clip plays faster than life. The speed-up is a frequency ratio and does not depend on the law: the swing's period, 1.20836 ± 0.00002 s from 19 zero crossings with no law at all, against the 6.009 s of an 8.97 m pendulum, gives 4.973× (the fit gives 4.972×). Its ± 0.025 is the 1% assumed on the stated 8.97 m length; the statistical part is ± 0.0015 from the fit, ± 0.0001 from the crossings.

truth.note: Real footage of the same pendulum, from a stretch the filmmaker sped up 5× and labelled on screen; we cropped the label out before the run. The length (8.97 m) and period (6.0 s) are the figures the filmmaker published with the video on Wikimedia Commons; Ansatz was told the length and nothing else. Re-run on 2 November with the pivot gate: the circle beside the path is refused as a pivot, so the swing is measured as the distance along its line, not as an angle about a centre to the side. The earlier run, on 29 October, measured that angle and read 4.98×.

gravity as the clip plays (25 × 9.81 if it runs 5× fast)

periodCheck.note: The speed-up is a frequency ratio, so it does not depend on the law. With no law at all, the 19 upward crossings of the swing's mean line in the stored distance-along-the-line series fall on a straight line in time to 0.4 ms: the period is 1.20836 ± 0.00002 s. An 8.97 m pendulum at standard gravity swings in 2π√(8.97 / 9.80665) = 6.0092 s, so the clip plays 4.973× faster than life (the fit's law gives 4.972×). Its uncertainty is almost all the stated length: ± 0.025 if the 8.97 m is good to 1%, against ± 0.0001 from the period (the fit alone gives ± 0.0015). The same film's real-time stretch, timed the same way (7 crossings), swings in 6.026 ± 0.009 s, 0.29% longer than 2π√(8.97 / 9.80665), as if the pendulum were about 0.6% longer than stated; the ratio of the two periods, which needs neither the length nor g, is 4.987 ± 0.007. Computed by scripts/period-check.ts from the stored series; no model call.
